EMPLOYEE INVENTION ASSIGNMENT — STATUTORY LIMITS AND SHOP RIGHT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Employee Invention Assignment — Statutory Limits and Shop Right Information Sheet is prepared with reference to Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC. It describes two things California law does with an invention-assignment provision like the one in an Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement between Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC: first, a statutory limit on which inventions such a provision can validly reach at all (California Labor Code §§ 2870–2872), and second, a separate common-law doctrine — the "shop right" — under which Acme Innovations LLC can hold an implied, nonexistent-in-writing, nonexclusive license to use an invention Jordan Lee made using Acme Innovations LLC's time or materials, independent of whether any assignment provision applies to that invention at all. This sheet is an informational record only. It does not itself determine whether any specific invention created by Jordan Lee falls inside or outside the statutory carve-out described below, does not determine whether a shop right exists as to any specific invention, and does not modify, waive, or supersede the terms of any assignment agreement actually signed by Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC.

THE STATUTORY LIMIT ON WHAT INVENTIONS CAN BE REQUIRED TO BE ASSIGNED
California Labor Code § 2870 places a limit on what an invention-assignment provision — the kind of clause that appears in an Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement between Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC — can validly require. By its terms, such a provision does not apply to an invention Jordan Lee developed entirely on Jordan Lee's own time, without using Acme Innovations LLC's equipment, supplies, facilities, or trade secret information, unless the invention either (1) relates, at the time of conception or reduction to practice, to Acme Innovations LLC's business, or to Acme Innovations LLC's actual or demonstrably anticipated research or development, or (2) results from work Jordan Lee performed for Acme Innovations LLC. Subdivision (b) then states the consequence: to the extent an assignment provision purports to reach an invention that subdivision (a) excludes, that provision is against the public policy of California and is unenforceable to that extent — the rest of the agreement is not necessarily affected.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Any provision in an employment agreement which provides that an employee shall assign, or offer to assign, any of his or her rights in an invention to his or her employer shall not apply to an invention that the employee developed entirely on his or her own time without using the employer’s equipment, supplies, facilities, or trade secret information except for those inventions that either: (1) Relate at the time of conception or reduction to practice of the invention to the employer’s business, or actual or demonstrably anticipated research or development of the employer; or (2) Result from any work performed by the employee for the employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory carve-out for inventions developed on the employee's own time (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2870.)
  "(b) To the extent a provision in an employment agreement purports to require an employee to assign an invention otherwise excluded from being required to be assigned under subdivision (a), the provision is against the public policy of this state and is unenforceable."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(b) (California Legislative Information text), unenforceability of a provision that reaches an excluded invention (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2870.)
  Known gap: The exclusion in subdivision (a) is cumulative, not alternative: an invention loses the exclusion (and can validly be required to be assigned) if it was developed using any of the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities, or trade secret information, even if it has nothing to do with the employer's business — and separately, even an invention developed with none of those resources loses the exclusion if it relates to the employer's business or actual or demonstrably anticipated research or development, or results from work performed for the employer. Whether a specific invention meets these fact-dependent conditions — what counts as the employee's "own time," what "relates to" the business means, what research is "demonstrably anticipated" — is not resolved by the statutory text itself and is not addressed by this document for any invention actually created by the employee named in this document. This section does not itself invalidate an entire assignment agreement; by its own terms it makes an offending provision unenforceable only to the extent it reaches an excluded invention, and it says nothing about whether an employer can require an employee to disclose an invention to test whether it qualifies for the exclusion (California courts have addressed disclosure obligations in this context, but that question was not independently verified in this research session and is not covered here).

THE EMPLOYER'S NOTICE REQUIREMENT — AND THE STATUTE'S SILENCE ON WHAT HAPPENS WITHOUT IT
California Labor Code § 2872 addresses employment agreements entered into after January 1, 1980 that contain an invention-assignment provision. Where such a provision is present — as in an agreement between Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC — the statute requires Acme Innovations LLC, at the time the agreement is made, to also provide Jordan Lee written notification that the agreement does not apply to an invention that qualifies fully under Labor Code § 2870. The same section places the burden of proof in any resulting suit or action on the employee claiming the benefit of that exclusion — meaning Jordan Lee, not Acme Innovations LLC, would bear the burden of showing that a given invention qualifies for the § 2870 carve-out.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If an employment agreement entered into after January 1, 1980, contains a provision requiring the employee to assign or offer to assign any of his or her rights in any invention to his or her employer, the employer must also, at the time the agreement is made, provide a written notification to the employee that the agreement does not apply to an invention which qualifies fully under the provisions of Section 2870. In any suit or action arising thereunder, the burden of proof shall be on the employee claiming the benefits of its provisions."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2872 (California Legislative Information text), the required written notification and burden of proof (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2872.)
  Known gap: Section 2872's text does not state what happens if an employer fails to give the required written notification — no invalidation of the assignment provision, no separate penalty, and no other stated consequence for noncompliance appears anywhere in the section as fetched and verified for this document. This document did not locate, and does not assert, any consequence for a missing § 2872 notice beyond what the statute's own text says (nothing) — that silence should not be read as either "the notice requirement is toothless" or "noncompliance has no legal significance"; the statute simply does not address it, and this document takes no position on how a court might treat noncompliance. Separately, § 2872 does not specify a required form for the written notification (e.g., a standalone notice versus language embedded in the assignment agreement itself), and that question is not addressed here.

THE SHOP RIGHT DOCTRINE — AN EMPLOYER'S IMPLIED NONEXCLUSIVE LICENSE
Separate from any written assignment provision, and separate from Labor Code § 2870's limits on what such a provision can require, courts recognize a common-law doctrine sometimes called the "shop right." The U.S. Supreme Court described it in United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp.: where an employee, during working hours and using the employer's materials and appliances, conceives and perfects an invention for which the employee (not the employer) obtains a patent, the employee must accord the employer a nonexclusive right to practice — that is, to use — that invention. This is an implied right that can arise from the circumstances of how the invention was made, without depending on any signed assignment agreement between Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Recognition of the nature of the act of invention also defines the limits of the so-called shop right, which, shortly stated, is that, where a servant, during his hours of employment, working with his master's materials and appliances, conceives and perfects an invention for which he obtains a patent, he must accord his master a nonexclusive right to practice the invention."
  — United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp., 289 U.S. 178, 188 (1933) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/102083/united-states-v-dubilier-condenser-corp/)
  Known gap: Dubilier is a 1933 U.S. Supreme Court decision applying general federal common-law principles to a dispute over patents obtained by federal government radio-laboratory employees; it is not a California case, and this research session did not independently verify a California appellate decision applying the shop-right doctrine on facts involving a private employer. The quoted passage is the Court's own general description of the shop-right doctrine as then already "settled as respects private employment" (citing 19th-century precedent), not language specific to any particular company's or employee's circumstances, and it does not itself decide whether a shop right exists for any invention the employee named in this document may have made. This corpus separately cites Dubilier's distinct holding about an employee "hired to invent" being bound to assign the resulting patent (clause patentassign_hired_to_invent in another document); that holding and this shop-right passage address different fact patterns within the same opinion and should not be conflated — the shop-right passage applies to an employee whose employment does not itself contemplate inventing, while the "hired to invent" holding applies where it does.

SHOP RIGHT IS A LICENSE TO USE, NOT OWNERSHIP OF THE INVENTION
The same Dubilier opinion draws a sharp line between the shop right and ownership of the invention itself. Because a shop right rests on equitable principles — the employer having supplied the time, facilities, and materials used to reach the result — the employer is entitled to use what was built with its own resources. But that entitlement does not extend to the invention's ownership: the opinion states that the employer "has no equity to demand a conveyance of the invention," which remains the property of the employee who conceived it, together with the patent right to exclude others (other than the employer) from it. A shop right is therefore narrower than an assignment: it gives Acme Innovations LLC, where it applies, a nonexclusive right to use an invention Jordan Lee made with Acme Innovations LLC's time or materials, without giving Acme Innovations LLC title to the invention or the right to stop Jordan Lee from licensing or using it elsewhere (subject to any separate confidentiality or trade secret obligations, which this clause does not address).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Since the servant uses his master's time, facilities, and materials to attain a concrete result, the latter is in equity entitled to use that which embodies his own property and to duplicate it as often as he may find occasion to employ similar appliances in his business. But the employer in such a case has no equity to demand a conveyance of the invention, which is the original conception of the employee alone, in which the employer had no part. This remains the property of him who conceived it, together with the right conferred by the patent, to exclude all others than the employer from the accruing benefits. These principles are settled as respects private employment."
  — United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp., 289 U.S. 178, 188-89 (1933) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/102083/united-states-v-dubilier-condenser-corp/)
  Known gap: This is the same 1933 U.S. Supreme Court opinion cited in the companion clause inventionlimits_shop_right_definition in this document — both citations come from a single source, independently re-verified for this specific point (the ownership/license distinction) rather than reused from the earlier quote, but they are not two separate sources. This passage describes the shop right's effect where it applies; it does not itself establish that a shop right exists for any invention the employee named in this document may have made, and it does not address how a shop right interacts with a written assignment provision that Labor Code § 2870 excludes from applying to a given invention — that interaction (whether an employer can hold a shop right to use an invention that § 2870 says it cannot require to be assigned) was not addressed in the text of § 2870 itself and was not independently verified against case law in this research session.
